sentences.text: Modern mass estimates for D. carnegii range from 12 to 14.8 metric tons. Diplodocus had small, forward-pointing, peg-like teeth located only in the front sections of the jaws. It also possessed a small braincase and a neck composed of at least 15 vertebrae.

The first fossils of Diplodocus were discovered in 1877 by S. W. Williston at Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado, alongside Benjamin Mudge. Othniel Charles Marsh named the first specimen Diplodocus longus in 1878, referring to the double-beamed chevron bones on the tail underside.

Remains of Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus found in the same strata suggest they coexisted with Diplodocus. Marsh and Hatcher assumed Diplodocus was aquatic due to the position of its nasal openings, but a 1951 study by Kenneth A. Kermack indicates sauropods likely could not breathe through nostrils when submerged due to water pressure. Reconstructions show Diplodocus had great pneumaticity in the neck and thorax, which could have aided respiration.

The type species of Diplodocus is D. longus, which is considered a nomen dubium. Subspecies include D. carnegii and D. hallorum, the latter originally classified as Seismosaurus. Seismosaurus is a synonym of Diplodocus. Diplodocus is the type genus and namesake of the family Diplodocidae.

Diplodocus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Kimmeridgian stage, between 154 and 152 million years ago. Diplodocus fossils have been found in what is now North America and Teruel, Spain. Diplodocus was one of the most common dinosaurs in the upper layers of the Morrison Formation.

It is debated whether the Diplodocus tail served a defensive, noisemaking, or tactile function. Detailed analysis suggests the original type specimen of Diplodocus longus is dubious. A proposal to change the type species of Diplodocus to D. carnegii was rejected by the ICZN because Hatcher failed to prove D. carnegii was distinct from D. longus. In 2015, Tschopp et al. classified the first complete diplodocid skull as an indeterminate diplodocine due to a lack of overlap with diagnostic Diplodocus postcranial material.
